a. Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.

For example, express the calculation "Subtract y from 5" as 5 - y.

b. Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.

For example, describe the expression 2 (8 + 7) as a product of two factors; view (8 + 7) as both a single entity and a sum of two terms.

c. Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).

For example, use the formulas V = s3 and A = 6 s2 to find the volume and surface area of a cube with sides of length s = 1/2.

Functions describe situations where one quantity determines another. the return on $10,000 invested at an annualized percentage rate of 4.25% is a function of the length of time the money is invested. Because we continually make theories about dependencies between quantities in nature and society, functions are important tools in the construction of mathematical models. In school mathematics, functions usually have numerical inputs and outputs and are often defined by an algebraic expression. a car to drive 100 miles is a function of the car's speed in miles per hour, v; the rule T ( v ) = 100/ v expresses this relationship algebraically and defines a function whose name is T. The set of inputs to a function is called its domain. We often infer the domain to be all inputs for which the expression defining a function has a value, or for which the function makes sense in a given context. A function can be described in various ways, such as by a graph (e.g., the trace of a seismograph); by a verbal rule, as in, "I'll give you a state, you give me the capital city;" by an algebraic expression like f ( x ) = a + bx; or by a recursive rule. The graph of a function is often a useful way of visualizing the relationship of the function models, and manipulating a mathematical expression for a function can throw light on the function's properties. Functions presented as expressions can model many important phenomena. Two important families of functions characterized by laws of growth are linear functions, which grow at a constant rate, and exponential functions, which grow at a constant percent rate. Linear functions with a constant term of zero describe proportional relationships. A graphing utility or a computer algebra system can be used to experiment with properties of these functions and their graphs and to build computational models of functions, including recursively defined functions.

Functions describe situations where one quantity determines another. the return on $10,000 invested at an annualized percentage rate of 4.25% is a function of the length of time the money is invested. Because we continually make theories about dependencies between quantities in nature and society, functions are important tools in the construction of mathematical models. In school mathematics, functions usually have numerical inputs and outputs and are often defined by an algebraic expression. a car to drive 100 miles is a function of the car's speed in miles per hour, v; the rule T ( v ) = 100/ v expresses this relationship algebraically and defines a function whose name is T. The set of inputs to a function is called its domain. We often infer the domain to be all inputs for which the expression defining a function has a value, or for which the function makes sense in a given context. A function can be described in various ways, such as by a graph (e.g., the trace of a seismograph); by a verbal rule, as in, "I'll give you a state, you give me the capital city;" by an algebraic expression like f ( x ) = a + bx; or by a recursive rule. The graph of a function is often a useful way of visualizing the relationship of the function models, and manipulating a mathematical expression for a function can throw light on the function's properties. Functions presented as expressions can model many important phenomena. Two important families of functions characterized by laws of growth are linear functions, which grow at a constant rate, and exponential functions, which grow at a constant percent rate. Linear functions with a constant term of zero describe proportional relationships. A graphing utility or a computer algebra system can be used to experiment with properties of these functions and their graphs and to build computational models of functions, including recursively defined functions.

mappings.statement:
Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume.

a. mappings.statement: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, thirds, half of, a third of, etc., and describe the whole as two halves, three thirds, four fourths. Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape. (1) Students develop an understanding of the meanings of multiplication and division of whole numbers through activities and problems involving equal-sized groups, arrays, and area models; multiplication is finding an unknown product, and division is finding an unknown factor in these situations. For equal-sized group situations, division can require finding the unknown number of groups or the unknown group size. Students use properties of operations to calculate products of whole numbers, using increasingly sophisticated strategies based on these properties to solve multiplication and division problems involving single-digit factors. By comparing a variety of solution strategies, students learn the relationship between multiplication and division. (2) Students develop an understanding of fractions, beginning with unit fractions. Students view fractions in general as being built out of unit fractions, and they use fractions along with visual fraction models to represent parts of a whole. Students understand that the size of a fractional part is relative to the size of the whole. paint in a small bucket could be less paint than 1/3 of the paint in a larger bucket, but 1/3 of a ribbon is longer than 1/5 of the same ribbon because when the ribbon is divided into 3 equal parts, the parts are longer than when the ribbon is divided into 5 equal parts. Students are able to use fractions to represent numbers equal to, less than, and greater than one. They solve problems that involve comparing fractions by using visual fraction models and strategies based on noticing equal numerators or denominators. (3) Students recognize area as an attribute of two-dimensional regions. They measure the area of a shape by finding the total number of samesize units of area required to cover the shape without gaps or overlaps, a square with sides of unit length being the standard unit for measuring area. Students understand that rectangular arrays can be decomposed into identical rows or into identical columns. By decomposing rectangles into rectangular arrays of squares, students connect area to multiplication, and justify using multiplication to determine the area of a rectangle. (4) Students describe, analyze, and compare properties of twodimensional shapes. They compare and classify shapes by their sides and angles, and connect these with definitions of shapes. Students also relate their fraction work to geometry by expressing the area of part of a shape as a unit fraction of the whole.

mappings.statement: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties. (1) Students use reasoning about multiplication and division to solve ratio and rate problems about quantities. By viewing equivalent ratios and rates as deriving from, and extending, pairs of rows (or columns) in the multiplication table, and by analyzing simple drawings that indicate the relative size of quantities, students connect their understanding of multiplication and division with ratios and rates. Thus students expand the scope of problems for which they can use multiplication and division to solve problems, and they connect ratios and fractions. Students solve a wide variety of problems involving ratios and rates. (2) Students use the meaning of fractions, the meanings of multiplication and division, and the relationship between multiplication and division to understand and explain why the procedures for dividing fractions make sense. Students use these operations to solve problems. Students extend their previous understandings of number and the ordering of numbers to the full system of rational numbers, which includes negative rational numbers, and in particular negative integers. They reason about the order and absolute value of rational numbers and about the location of points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. (3) Students understand the use of variables in mathematical expressions. They write expressions and equations that correspond to given situations, evaluate expressions, and use expressions and formulas to solve problems. Students understand that expressions in different forms can be equivalent, and they use the properties of operations to rewrite expressions in equivalent forms. Students know that the solutions of an equation are the values of the variables that make the equation true. Students use properties of operations and the idea of maintaining the equality of both sides of an equation to solve simple one-step equations. Students construct and analyze tables, such as tables of quantities that are in equivalent ratios, and they use equations (such as 3 x = y ) to describe relationships between quantities. (4) Building on and reinforcing their understanding of number, students begin to develop their ability to think statistically. Students recognize that a data distribution may not have a definite center and that different ways to measure center yield different values. The median measures center in the sense that it is roughly the middle value. The mean measures center in the sense that it is the value that each data point would take on if the total of the data values were redistributed equally, and also in the sense that it is a balance point. Students recognize that a measure of variability (interquartile median yet be distinguished by their variability. Students learn to describe and summarize numerical data sets, identifying clusters, peaks, gaps, and symmetry, considering the context in which the data were collected. Students in Grade 6 also build on their work with area in elementary school by reasoning about relationships among shapes to determine area, surface area, and volume. They find areas of right triangles, other triangles, and special quadrilaterals by decomposing these shapes, rearranging or removing pieces, and relating the shapes to rectangles. Using these methods, students discuss, develop, and justify formulas for areas of triangles and parallelograms. Students find areas of polygons and surface areas of prisms and pyramids by decomposing them into pieces whose area they can determine. They reason about right rectangular prisms with fractional side lengths to extend formulas for the volume of a right rectangular prism to fractional side lengths. They prepare for work on scale drawings and constructions in Grade 7 by drawing polygons in the coordinate plane.

(1) Students use linear equations and systems of linear equations to represent, analyze, and solve a variety of problems. Students recognize equations for proportions ( y / x = m or y = mx ) as special linear equations ( y = mx + b ), understanding that the constant of proportionality ( m ) is the slope, and the graphs are lines through the origin. They understand that the slope ( m ) of a line is a constant rate of change, so that if the input or x -coordinate changes by an amount A, the output or y -coordinate changes by the amount m·A. Students also use a linear equation to describe the association between two quantities in bivariate data (such as arm span vs. height for students in a classroom). At this grade, fitting the model, and assessing its fit to the data are done informally. Interpreting the model in the context of the data requires students to express a relationship between the two quantities in question and to interpret components of the relationship (such as slope and y -intercept) in terms of the situation. Students strategically choose and efficiently implement procedures to solve linear equations in one variable, understanding that when they use the properties of equality and the concept of logical equivalence, they maintain the solutions of the original equation. Students solve systems of two linear equations in two variables and relate the systems to pairs of lines in the plane; these intersect, are parallel, or are the same line. Students use linear equations, systems of linear equations, linear functions, and their understanding of slope of a line to analyze situations and solve problems. Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events. (1) Students use linear equations and systems of linear equations to represent, analyze, and solve a variety of problems. Students recognize equations for proportions ( y / x = m or y = mx ) as special linear equations ( y = mx + b ), understanding that the constant of proportionality ( m ) is the slope, and the graphs are lines through the origin. Students use linear equations, systems of linear equations, linear functions, and their understanding of slope of a line to analyze situations and solve problems. Students show that the sum of the angles in a triangle is the angle formed by a straight line, and that various configurations of lines give rise to similar triangles because of the angles created when a transversal cuts parallel lines. Students understand the statement of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse, and can explain why the Pythagorean Theorem holds, square in two different ways. They apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find distances between points on the coordinate plane, to find lengths, and to analyze polygons. Students recognize equations for proportions ( y / x = m or y = mx ) as special linear equations ( y = mx + b ), understanding that the constant of proportionality ( m ) is the slope, and the graphs are lines through the origin. They understand that the slope ( m ) of a line is a constant rate of change, so that if the input or x -coordinate changes by an amount A, the output or y -coordinate changes by the amount m·A. Students also use a linear equation to describe the association between two quantities in bivariate data (such as arm span vs. height for students in a classroom). At this grade, fitting the model, and assessing its fit to the data are done informally. Students strategically choose and efficiently implement procedures to solve linear equations in one variable, understanding that when they use the properties of equality and the concept of logical equivalence, they maintain the solutions of the original equation. Students solve systems of two linear equations in two variables and relate the systems to pairs of lines in the plane; these intersect, are parallel, or are the same line. mappings.statement:
Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.

a. Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.

b. Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.

c. Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.

For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?

mappings.statement: Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered. (1) Students extend their understanding of ratios and develop understanding of proportionality to solve single- and multi-step problems. Students use their understanding of ratios and proportionality to solve a wide variety of percent problems, including those involving discounts, interest, taxes, tips, and percent increase or decrease. Students solve problems about scale drawings by relating corresponding lengths between the objects or by using the fact that relationships of lengths within an object are preserved in similar objects. Students graph proportional relationships and understand the unit rate informally as a measure of the steepness of the related line, called the slope. They distinguish proportional relationships from other relationships. (2) Students develop a unified understanding of number, recognizing fractions, decimals (that have a finite or a repeating decimal representation), and percents as different representations of rational numbers. Students extend addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division to all rational numbers, maintaining the properties of operations and the relationships between addition and subtraction, and multiplication and division. By applying these properties, and by viewing negative numbers in terms of everyday contexts (e.g., amounts owed or temperatures below zero), students explain and interpret the rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing with negative numbers. They use the arithmetic of rational numbers as they formulate expressions and equations in one variable and use these equations to solve problems. (3) Students continue their work with area from Grade 6, solving problems involving the area and circumference of a circle and surface area of threedimensional objects. In preparation for work on congruence and similarity in Grade 8 they reason about relationships among two-dimensional figures using scale drawings and informal geometric constructions, and they gain familiarity with the relationships between angles formed by intersecting lines. Students work with three-dimensional figures, relating them to twodimensional figures by examining cross-sections. They solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes and right prisms. (4) Students build on their previous work with single data distributions to compare two data distributions and address questions about differences between populations. They begin informal work with random sampling

data.rationale: Beyond its role through membership semantics, correctly construing direction and strictness directly governs which side of a boundary and whether an endpoint enters the reported set; retained as a direct support edge rather than a second gate to avoid asserting redundant blocking structure.

A complete solution set is definitionally the set of all and only admissible values that satisfy the original inequality, so satisfaction-based membership is the correctness and completeness criterion of the target rather than a preferred solving procedure; a learner without it cannot determine or bound the set as complete.

On the algebraic route named in ev003, accepting a rewritten inequality as having the original solution set rests on solution-set preservation; it is non-blocking because direct order reasoning, tables, graphs, and authorized technology reach the target without any rewrite.

The truth condition invoked by satisfaction membership is definitionally the displayed directed, strict-or-inclusive comparison evaluated under one common assignment; without that comparison semantics the membership equivalence is not well-defined.

Distinguishing a fixed parameter from a varying input presupposes viewing the quadratic as an input-output relation, though the task's notation conventions may make the distinction directly available.

A stable input-variable-to-quantity correspondence supports interpretations involving reference inputs, shifts, per-unit scales, and units, but is often supplied directly and is not independently assessed in every instance.

Knowing what the parameter position controls in the supplied form is what makes the contextual mapping possible, but a task may state that role directly, so it is strong support rather than a reliably blocking gate.

Identifying the whole quantity the quadratic expression models supplies the contextual referent against which one parameter's role is interpreted; it is conditional because the task may label that quantity explicitly.

Reading the quadratic representation as an input-output assignment rather than a fixed number underlies any claim that a parameter shapes how the output quantity depends on the input; it is retained as non-blocking support because the task establishes the function.
When the supplied form contains a nested part, recognizing that part as one quantity helps locate what the parameter modifies; it is not exercised when the parameter position is already delimited.
Analyzing a supplied model normally requires preserving its contextual input-output meaning; the edge is left non-hard because the correspondence may be fully labeled within the task.
This terminal capability is an explicit component of the target outcome; the panel omitted only the final outcome link.

Knowing what makes a function quadratic supports judging whether that family fits the situation, but the task may characterize the family verbally so the structural recognition is not definitionally required.

Recognizing the supplied rule's degree-two structure can inform the analysis, but it is unnecessary when the task already identifies the model as quadratic or supplies only a graphical or tabular form.
When the compared implication is a rate or difference pattern, the second-difference invariant supplies its meaning; most other comparisons do not exercise it.
Agreement or conflict between a quadratic-family implication and supplied contextual evidence can warrant the family judgment, though a structural contextual rationale may be supplied directly.
Consistency can depend on whether the implicated input is contextually admissible, but some comparisons concern an input already established as admissible.

A family-level judgment is meaningful only relative to which contextual quantity depends on which, but authored tasks frequently label the roles explicitly, so the dependency is not reliably blocking.
Constant second differences in exact equal-step data are one optional diagnostic supporting a quadratic-family determination; other tasks supply a mechanism or graph-based rationale instead.
The same quadratic rule can be appropriate on one contextual domain and inappropriate on another, but domain identification is conditional when the domain is stated with the model.
A quadratic model may be suitable only over the contextual input range under consideration, yet many tasks supply the domain directly rather than requiring its identification.

Most appropriateness analyses rest on one or more implication-condition comparisons, but a purely structural or mechanism-based analysis is also admissible, so the relation is strong support rather than a mandated constituent.
An implication and a contextual condition must refer to corresponding quantities and units, although a task may assert that correspondence within the comparison itself.
Taking a/b of the quantity and then the complement is a complete optional route to the part:whole outcome and is never required.
The learner must compare the designated part with the whole rather than with the other part; conflating the two conditions changes the defining relation and is the characteristic blocking failure.
Unit-share reasoning is one complete optional route to the part:part outcome and is never required.

When the share value or a part is generated from a supplied correspondence rather than read off, this reused representation-neutral missing-quantity capability performs the numerical determination; it is optional because the parts may be obtained by other exact reasoning.
Reversing the ordered roles, or treating the second term as the whole, changes the defining constraint and makes a correct determination impossible.
The reported values satisfy the target only if they jointly compose the given quantity, so the composition condition is definitional rather than strategic.
This terminal capability is an explicit component of the target outcome; the panel omitted only the final outcome link.
Once the designated part is fixed by its relation to the whole, the second reported value is defined as its complement, so the composition relation is definitionally required.
The share-value route rests on the fact that scaling both ratio terms by the same share value preserves the specified relation.
The fraction-of-the-whole route may be executed as a supplied proportion such as x/a = Q/(a+b) or x/a = Q/b, in which case the reused atom supplies the computation; it remains non-blocking.
Treating the whole as b shares is one complete optional route to the part:whole outcome and is never required.

Recognising that satisfying parts are common multiples of the ratio terms grounds why scaled pairs meet the condition, but a learner may instead take fractions of the whole without articulating the invariance.
Evaluating a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the quantity is a second complete optional route, retained so that no single method is privileged.

The power-of-ten route only yields an admissible result because its numerator is an integer and its power-of-ten denominator is a nonzero integer; the validity concept supplies that criterion without prescribing the route.

The fraction's unit-fraction value meaning grounds the equivalence condition the conversion must preserve, but it is non-blocking: its confirmed scope is nonnegative conventional fractions, and a learner may verify equivalence by a quotient reading or another exact route.

For finite-decimal inputs, the power-of-ten rewriting is one complete optional route satisfying the target; place-value, quotient, and scaling routes are equally admissible, so the route is not a hard prerequisite.

The output-form criterion is definitional: a response satisfies the target only if it is an integer numerator over a nonzero integer denominator, so distinguishing valid from invalid fraction form is constitutive of the conversion rather than one optional method. The edge imposes no positive-denominator convention, lowest-terms condition, or notation layout.
For whole-number inputs, constructing n/1 is one complete optional route that satisfies the target; other exact equivalent fractions are equally admissible, so it is never a prerequisite.

Explaining what a correspondence between two modeled input-output situations means requires interpreting each of those situations under the context's established quantity roles, units, and domain; the target is definitionally the relational case of that same contextual semantics.

Reading a symmetry correspondence as pairing input-output pairs of the same function is easier when graph points and symbolic pairs are recognized as denoting the same assignment, but the correspondence can also be stated and recognized entirely within one representation.

Knowing which function pairs the established symmetry relates, and what output relation that pairing does or does not license, is the definitional mathematical content of the statement whose contextual implication the target explains; without it the contextual explanation has no determinate content.

Recognizing that a graph point, table entry, or symbolic pair denotes the same directed input-output assignment grounds treating a supplied pair as one interpretable correspondence, but it is non-blocking because a task may present the pair already labeled with its contextual roles.

Reading a one-digit partner as zero tens and some ones is needed only under the mixed-addend profile that ev001 names; it is irrelevant to the two-two-digit paradigm case, so it is a conditional support rather than a reliably blocking dependency.

Mapping each established root occurrence to its correctly signed linear factor is definitional for a root-based factored representation and reliably blocks construction when absent.

Assigning the mathematical negative side to the context's direction, category, or state is one of the two semantic constituents of the target response, the other being the amount; every complete interpretation contains this mapping.

The generic opposite-side relation supports mapping the negative side onto contextual opposites, but the specific contextual convention must still be supplied by or inferred from the situation, so this is supporting rather than definitional.

Decoding a conventional negative numeral is exercised when the value is presented symbolically; it is not a universal gate because the target admits verbal, labelled-scale, tabular, and diagrammatic presentations whose signed meaning is already accessible.

The explicitly required output is the equation of a vertical line, so the equivalence between a fixed horizontal coordinate and x=c is definitionally necessary.
The target depends definitionally on knowing what makes a candidate vertical line the reflection axis of the represented parabola rather than an arbitrary vertical line.
Reading a horizontal coordinate against a calibrated axis relies on the common-unit horizontal metric, but a labeled gridline reading may be performed without separate structural recognition.
Learners customarily read fixed horizontal coordinates before adopting the x=c convention, but neither capability blocks the other.
Equal horizontal distance on either side of a vertical line presupposes the orthogonal, common-unit coordinate metric, though gestalt symmetry recognition does not require articulating it.

Treating the reflected locations as genuine points of the quadratic's graph gives the reflection correspondence its mathematical content, but the symmetry judgment can be made visually without a separate membership response.

The target artifact is a function relating two quantities, so the directed one-output-per-input correspondence and the fixed quantity roles are definitional to the produced object; a rule written without that semantics may be an exponential expression but not a function of the designated input.

Function-correspondence semantics supports assigning the two quantities to input and output roles during interpretation, but is non-blocking there because a task may state the roles directly.

Assigning factor, interval, reference, and baseline roles as exponential roles is definitionally dependent on the repeated-multiplication relation for equal input increments; without it the same information can only be read additively.
Plain data encoding customarily precedes model-data encoding in the evidenced sequence, but it is not definitionally required for it.

A coefficient or augmented matrix is defined by the placement of equation coefficients and constants into ordered rows and columns, so the indexing relation is definitionally prior.
Declaring the variable and equation orders supports system encoding when they are not supplied, but selecting them is not a definitional gate because tasks commonly fix them.
Declaring the orientation and category order supports dataset encoding when the task does not prescribe a layout, but it is not exercised when the schema is supplied.
Encoding plain rectangular data customarily precedes encoding an algebraic system, but the system branch can be established directly from its own convention, so the relation is ordering only.

Interpreting the amount-and-unit relation keeps the answer a measurement in the given unit, but it is routed to the target as support because its contribution reaches the outcome through the representation and unit-bearing product atoms rather than as an independent gate.
The unit-bearing product cannot be determined without determining the whole-number coefficient g × m; unit retention alone supplies no numerical value.

Retaining U in the product depends on treating mU as an amount in unit U rather than as a bare numeral, so the scalar-product atom applies this concept rather than gating on a separate demonstration of it.

Assigning the factor roles uses the meaning of mU as one unit-bearing measurement distinguished from the dimensionless count, but the concept need not be separately demonstrated when the task labels the quantities.

Solving an otherwise unspecified one-step measurement problem by multiplication definitionally requires mapping its quantities and unknown onto the multiplication relation rather than another operation.

Every adjacent transition in a backward-by-tens continuation is by definition an application of the bounded ten-less relation, so reliably producing one valid ten-less step blocks or enables the repeated-step capability.
The by-ones route is defined as ten iterations of the immediate-predecessor relation within 120, so that relation is definitionally required for this strategy (though not for the target itself).

Recognising that ten less lowers the tens count by one and leaves the ones unchanged makes the one-step relation generalisable to anchors with any ones value, but the relation can also be recalled or counted out, so the dependency is supporting rather than blocking.
Taking ten tracked single backward steps is one optional route to the same ten-less relation and is never required for the target.

Fluency with the descending decade sequence gives a familiar reference for ten-less transitions at multiples of ten, but it does not cover anchors with nonzero ones values and is not definitionally required.
The multiple-of-ten case is the narrower special case usually established before general anchors, but the general capability subsumes it and does not logically depend on rote decade recitation.
The explanation's content is the correspondence between the two sign categories and the context's opposite pair, so recognising that pair is definitionally required.

A signed value's contextual meaning is one member of the situation's opposite pair, so the pair must be recognised before a sign can be mapped onto one of its members; magnitude comparison is not involved.

Naming the situation's baseline strengthens and often frames the paired explanation in reference-relative contexts, but the target does not require an explanation of zero and can be met in polarity contexts without one.

Knowing the baseline or neutral state materially helps interpret signs in reference-relative contexts such as temperature and elevation, but it is not a universal gate, since polarity contexts such as credit/debit or electric charge can be interpreted from the stated convention alone.
Explaining the joint use of both sign categories requires interpreting what a signed value means in the presented context; the target is broader only in relating both meanings as an opposite pair.

Parameter-role interpretation presupposes knowing which contextual quantity is the input and which the modeled output, while the parameter roles themselves remain a distinct recognition object.

Interpreting which supplied information fills the reference, factor, interval, and exponent roles is part of articulating the procedure, but it is non-blocking because a task may present the roles already labeled or supply a complete exponential form.

Assigning contextual input and output roles uses the directed-correspondence meaning of a function, though many contexts make the dependence evident without separately eliciting that concept.

Exact rational multiplication is invoked by most direct and transformed evaluations, including reciprocal and common-denominator routes, but a holistic or cancellation-based route need not display it separately.

Exact rational addition is the reusable computational component invoked whenever an addition appears in an in-scope numerator, denominator, or surrounding expression; it is item-conditional because not every complex fraction contains addition.
Ordered subtraction of fraction-form operands definitionally presupposes reading each fraction as the exact rational value being differenced.

The validated nonnegative fraction-value interpretation is the attested subdomain of the broader integer-entry value interpretation; it is support, not a gate, because the broader capability may also be established directly on signed entries.

Every in-scope item requires reading its numerical fraction entries as exact rational values; without that reading no route can produce an equivalent value.

Reading a single fraction bar as a division relation is the attested simple case that the nested structural interpretation extends to complete subexpressions; it is support because a learner may read a fraction bar directly as a grouped quotient.

The validated nonnegative conventional-fraction quotient atom is the attested subdomain of the general exact rational division component; it is support because the general component may include signed or integer-valued operands it excludes.

Lowest-terms reduction supports final reporting when a simplified fraction is the required form, but it is unnecessary for an integer, an already reduced fraction, or another authorized evaluated form, and the evidence fixes no output convention.

Conventional precedence settles the internal order of a numerator or denominator containing more than one operation, but many in-scope subexpressions contain a single operation or explicit grouping, so the recognition is not blocking.
Adding values presented in fraction form definitionally presupposes reading each fraction as the exact rational value being combined.

Every complex fraction denotes at least one outer quotient of rational values, so this component is near-universal; it remains component_of rather than a hard prerequisite because a learner may resolve that quotient through a value-preserving global transformation whose final step is whole-number or integer division.
Exact multiplication of fraction-form operands definitionally presupposes the value meaning of each operand.
Exact ordered rational subtraction is the reusable component invoked whenever subtraction appears in an in-scope subexpression; it is item-conditional.

Every general algebraic formulation must contain symbols denoting the two varying quantities, so symbolic denotation is a constituent of the target performance; it is not modelled as a hard prerequisite because the task may supply the symbols or their assignments, in which case no separate denotation performance is blocking.

Having symbols available for the two quantities makes the symbolic statement of the fixed-multiplier relation (y = kx) readable, but the invariant-multiplier structure can be recognized from contextual, tabular, or graphical presentations without any symbolic labelling, so the relation is supporting only.

A single fixed multiplicative dependence is definitional of direct proportionality, so any correct equation or equivalent symbolic relation must encode that structure; without this recognition a syntactically similar relation (additive offset, varying rate) fails to represent the stated relationship, which makes the dependency definitional and reliably blocking.

The target's premise 'equal shares' must be read in the area sense for two-dimensional region models; otherwise the non-implication is indistinguishable from a claim about outlines. It is not a hard prerequisite because a task may state or mark the shares as equal-sized.

Recognizing that two share regions differ in shape supports evaluation of diagrammatic instances of the target, but it is not definitionally blocking because the shape difference may be stated or made explicit by the task.

Identifying that the two reference wholes match keeps the conclusion inside its intended scope and blocks confusion with comparisons across differently sized wholes; it is non-blocking because the identical-whole condition is often supplied and the evidence does not define a formal test for 'identical'.
Whether the designated region is half of, a third of, or a fourth of the whole is definitionally fixed by the total number of equal regions in that whole.

Halves, thirds, and fourths denote equal shares rather than any two, three, or four regions, so the naming atom uses the equal-area concept; independent verification is not blocking because target inputs are stipulated equal partitions.

Which plural share-class word applies is definitionally fixed by whether the equal partition contains two, three, or four regions, so for an arbitrary displayed partition the region count must be established.

Calling one region a half, a third, or a fourth of the figure uses the defining condition that the whole was divided into equal-area regions, without requiring the learner to verify equality on each target item.

Reading regions as parts of one whole makes the plural class word meaningful, but the class naming can be performed reliably from the region count alone without designating an individual region, so this is support rather than a gate.
A phrase such as 'a third of the rectangle' is meaningful only if the designated region is read as the part and the enclosing figure as the whole that the word 'of' refers to.
Source formulations list the plural class words before the singular 'of' phrases, suggesting a customary teaching order, but neither capability blocks the other and either may be established first.

Reading graph points as function information requires treating them as input-output pairs of one single-valued assignment.

Interpreting the table is the source-side constituent of every target instance whose source is a numerical table.

Interpreting the verbal description is the source-side constituent of every target instance whose source is verbal.
Interpreting the algebraic source is the source-side constituent of every target instance whose source is algebraic; it is conditional on the instance rather than blocking for all instances.

Producing a faithful table requires knowing its input-output pairing and completeness semantics.
Table realization is the destination-side constituent of every target instance whose destination is a numerical table.
A verbal description denotes a function only if read as specifying one output for each authorized input.

Pointwise evaluation makes the value-based hand route to the graph available, but it is route-conditional and therefore nonblocking, since transformation of an established parent graph, a supplied table, or authorized technology can produce the graph without it.

Evaluation supplies the function value that a membership judgment compares against, but the membership atom explicitly excludes evaluating an unfamiliar rule as its assessed action and can be exercised with supplied values, so the dependency is supportive rather than blocking.
Interpreting tens and ones supports inscribing decomposed numerical parts, but the inscription may record a non-place-value relation instead.

Identifying each number's components makes like-unit quantities available, though a task may supply pre-grouped components.
Drawings are the source-named recording medium and directly support the record, but the evidence does not fix them as strictly obligatory for every written numerical method.
Built groupings can be combined componentwise, but the combination can also proceed from numerically identified components.

Combining the ones components typically supplies the 10-through-18 ones quantity on which composition operates, though that quantity may already be presented.

Drawing the baseline two-addend relation is the general drawing capability that a strategy-step drawing elaborates; it is support rather than a gate because a strategy step may be drawn without first depicting the whole relation.

Viewing area as an exact count of non-overlapping unit squares supports the additive relation because the two component counts exhaust the whole count, but area additivity may also be grounded without unit-square counting.

A tile or array partition display is one optional medium for realising the target's two-region model; it is explicitly non-blocking because the target admits a labelled rectangle with no tiles or cells, and the target boundary excludes tiling as required evidence.

Associating the whole and the two component regions with a×(b+c), a×b, and a×c requires the rectangle-dimensions-to-product correspondence; without it the labels are not mathematically warranted, even when the numerical products are supplied.

Recognising that adjacent lengths b and c exhaust the composed side supports placing the single partition line in a tile or array display, though such a display may also be supplied already partitioned.

A valid model must preserve b and c as adjacent parts of the single side b+c; without that composition relation the geometric partition does not represent the stated expression a×(b+c), so the dependency is definitional rather than methodological.

The unit-square interpretation grounds why the represented rectangles carry area rather than mere array cardinality, but a learner may work from an already established side-length area relation without separately articulating this definition, so it is not reliably blocking.

Every adjacent step of a backward count is by definition an application of the immediate integer-predecessor relation, so failure on that one-step relation reliably blocks continuation of an arbitrary backward sequence, including passage through zero. The order structure around zero is what makes the predecessor determinate at 0 and on the negative side (-1 rather than 1 after 0; -2 rather than 0 after -1). It is support rather than a gate because a learner may answer these cases from a recalled sequence or a supplied oriented display without articulating the structure.

Sign interpretation helps preserve the meaning of produced negative terms when signed notation is used, but the outcome mandates no notation and may be met from an oriented display or recalled sequence, so it is conditional non-blocking support only.

The concept underwrites the explicitly scoped through-zero portion of the outcome, but it is conditional: sequences that stay on one side of zero do not exercise it, and no articulation of the structure is required in the response.

Reading a presented signed numeral's sign supports determining its predecessor when the input is a signed numeral, but it is not blocking because the input may be verbal, a marked number-line position, or otherwise already interpreted.

The inclusion holds precisely because the corresponding linear function produces each sequence term at an aligned allowed input; recognizing terms as outputs of that function is definitional content of the target, not an optional method.
The left-hand object of the target inclusion is definitionally the set of term values assigned to the sequence's authorized positions; without that reading the inclusion claim cannot be interpreted.

Equality of corresponding outputs is the constituent judgment the target-level table strategy aggregates in order to report a common ordered pair or a warranted status.
Knowing which entry of a record holds the first-variable role supports pairing records by that value, though an already aligned display can make the correspondence visually explicit.

The strategy relies on the tabular semantics that a listed record satisfies its equation and that a finite table need not list every solution, which is what makes a table match warrant a solution and blocks unwarranted absence inferences.
Locating records that share a first-variable value is a constituent action of analyzing two tables for common ordered pairs whenever the records are not already aligned.

An equality-preserving transformation is defined relative to the unknown, the fixed quantities, and the two complete sides being preserved, so those must be identifiable in the model first.

Producing an adequate comparison graph supplies the evidence the target analyzes, but it is not universally required because the graph may be supplied, partially completed, or generated with authorized technology.

Producing a comparison graph customarily precedes reading satisfaction from it, but the classification capability applies equally to supplied graphs, so no dependency is asserted.

Locating a designated feature's input value can help align the classified input with the correct graph location, but classification may be performed at a supplied or visually indicated input without any coordinate reading.

Layer-by-layer structural reading supports planning an isolation route, but a learner may reach the isolated form by recognized equivalent rewriting or by selecting among candidate forms.

Rearranging a formula by equation-solving reasoning is defined on the equality relation between its two sides; without that relation the target action has no object.
Reading the immediate containing operation supports selecting or understanding the corresponding reversible transformation, but the transformation may instead be supplied by the task.

A transformation applied to both sides operates on, and must preserve, an equality relation, so recognizing that relation is definitional.

The derivation must connect scaled boundary lengths to each figure's perimeter, which is impossible without the defining interpretation of perimeter as the complete additive boundary total; this holds for any admissible derivation route.

The preimage set is the candidate set most often screened by contextual restrictions, so it customarily precedes screening without being definitionally required, since candidates may be supplied or produced by another route.
Evaluation supplies the mathematical result for forward-value contextual questions but is not exercised for inverse, zero, or extremum questions, so it is not blocking.
A designated-extremum result supports contextual greatest-or-least questions when that feature is requested, and remains an optional non-blocking branch.
The represented query identifies which input's output is required in a forward-value application.

When the problem states restrictions such as a validity interval or a sign condition, screening the model-derived candidates is needed to produce an answer within context, but many tasks yield a single already admissible result.

Interpreting the established input-output pair supplies the contextual meaning of the determined result when the problem statement does not already fix it.
Preimage determination supports questions asking when a modeled quantity reaches a stated level or equals zero, and is one optional query branch among several.

Answering the contextual problem includes establishing which function relation the question asks about; it is a component rather than a hard prerequisite because the task may state the query explicitly.

Place-group analysis strongly supports interpreting structurally complex or unfamiliar number names, but it is not asserted as blocking because familiar names may be recognised lexically and the authorised naming convention is unresolved.

Within the provisional additive base-ten syntax, the value of an arbitrary expanded expression is determined by the contributions its terms denote, so interpreting individual terms is definitionally required rather than merely helpful; the claim is contingent on that syntax and is flagged in schema observations.

Reading an additive expanded expression as one number requires treating the displayed terms as contributions to a single total; a learner who reads them as separate unrelated numbers cannot recover the value, making this relation definitional for the representation as scoped.

Knowing what a digit contributes by position supports interpreting the same contribution when it is displayed as a separate expanded-form term, though the term notation itself must also be established.

Knowing that ten of one unit make one of the next higher unit grounds the meaning of named place units such as ten-thousands inside an expanded term, but term interpretation can also be established from an aligned place-value display without articulating the equivalence.

Positional-contribution knowledge supports mapping name groups onto base-ten places, but the language-specific lexical and scale-marker conventions add representational knowledge that numeral analysis does not supply.

Scale markers in number names presuppose the nested base-ten unit structure, but the mapping is largely a language convention that a learner may acquire lexically, so the edge is weak and non-blocking.
Identifying the two readings as one vector requires the componentwise reading to be available.
Judging whether a translated arrow represents the same vector requires first interpreting each arrow's direction and magnitude.
Componentwise addition definitionally depends on interpreting component positions relative to one established coordinate order or basis.
Identifying the two readings as one vector requires the geometric resultant reading to be available.
Translation equivalence makes tip-to-tail and parallelogram displays readable but is not required when the task supplies an already arranged resultant or a bound-vector display.
The geometric resultant relation is defined over directed vector arrows, so interpreting each addend and the resultant as a directed vector is definitional and reliably blocking.

Directed-arrow meaning is customarily established before coordinate components, but component-form interpretation can be established directly from an ordered basis, so the ordering is instructional rather than blocking.
Established quantity roles support translating a contextual datum into a directed function condition, though supplied symbolic labels may already encode the roles.
A condition's mathematical interpretation supports checking whether a candidate model satisfies it, though the condition may already be supplied mathematically.

Parameter determination supports construction whenever a parameterized exponential form is used, but it is route-conditional because parameters may be supplied or an authorized representation may be produced directly; it is therefore recorded as strong support rather than a required component.
Condition-level checking supports the appropriateness of the produced model, but an accurate construction need not display a separate verification step.
The constructed rule must belong to the exponential family under the applicable convention; the relation is conceptual rather than blocking because the task may supply the rule form directly.
Mathematically interpreted contextual conditions are what constrain the parameters of a supplied exponential form, although some tasks supply the constraints already in symbolic form.
Knowing which structural slots the established exponential form has supports determining its parameters, but the form and its parameter roles may simply be supplied with the task.
Interpreting the situation's stated information as model conditions supports producing a model that represents that situation, without being a separately required response.

A contextual one-variable inequality must carry one consistent association between its variable and the quantity that variable denotes; this association is an internal constituent of the created artifact.

When the supplied corresponding value is anchored at a nonzero input, computing b = a0 - d*n0 is an alternative accurate route to the fixed term that the zero-input determination would otherwise provide.

When the situation presents a dependent quantity varying with the designated variable, directed role identification keeps the modeled expression from reversing the two quantities; roles may instead be supplied, or the compared quantity may simply be a fixed bound.

When the situation explicitly supplies an admissibility condition, interpreting it supports preserving that condition with the created model; most instances supply no such condition, so the support is conditional and non-blocking.
The single comparison symbol of the created inequality must preserve both the contextual order direction and whether the boundary value is included.
An established zero-input value can supply the fixed term of the affine expression, but not every context establishes or requires a meaningful zero-input reference.
A determined constant rate can supply the variable coefficient of the affine expression, yet the rate may be stated outright or the expression may be assembled in another equivalent authorized form.

Knowing that the base occupies the fixed-step multiplier role clarifies what a stated relative change must be converted into, but the conversion can also be performed from the contextual statement alone.
The per-step multiplier role frames what the ratio of two outputs over an input difference recovers, though the recovery may proceed purely computationally.

Seeing a combined-ones quantity of ten through eighteen as one ten plus leftover ones makes the residual-ones outcome of the exchange determinate, but a learner may instead bundle ten ones physically and enumerate what remains.

Quantifying the combined ones (at most eighteen) is one accurate route to the threshold decision, but the decision can also be made by forming a complete group of ten from a model without stating any sum, so this is non-blocking.

Adjudicated against Luna's hard_prerequisite_for claim and in favour of Sol: recognising that the combined ones reach ten normally initiates the exchange, but a learner explicitly directed to compose a ten can execute the value-preserving exchange without independently making the threshold decision, so the dependency is ordering rather than definitional. The two atoms are co-required parts of the outcome.
Unit-preserving combination supplies the unnormalized tens-and-ones representation on which the composition operates, but a task may present that combined representation directly.

The target composition is defined as replacing ten ones by one ten without changing the total, so the quantity-preserving equivalence of those two unit forms is a definitional dependency; a learner who does not treat them as equal cannot preserve value through the exchange.
The ten-for-ten-ones equivalence grounds the ten inside the ten-and-leftover structure of a teen quantity, though the teen structure may also be known from familiar ten-frame or bundle experience.
A complete, gap-free, non-overlapping unit-cube packing of the prism is the concrete or spatial representation of the general volume-as-unit-cube-count relation.
Layer- or row-organised accumulation is one admissible way to obtain the exact packed-cube total; direct enumeration is equally admissible, so this route supports but never gates the target.

The target's stated method makes the complete gap-free unit-cube packing the object whose cardinality is counted; without an established complete packing (whether supplied, completed, or built) there is no collection whose count is the prism's volume, so the dependency is definitional rather than an instructional preference.
The layered route groups cubes of an actual packing, so an established complete packing is required before its layers can be organised and accumulated.
The axis-aligned right-triangle configuration is a constitutive part of this particular derivation route.
The route replaces the squared leg lengths with the squared coordinate separations, so the separation relations are a constitutive part of it.
The squared-length relation d^2 = h^2 + v^2 is the central inference of this route.

The separation pair supplies the leg lengths of the configuration, but a learner may construct or identify the auxiliary corner before expressing the separations symbolically, so the dependency is supporting rather than blocking.
The target formula necessarily relates distance to the differences of corresponding coordinates, whichever valid derivation route is used.
Reading an absolute coordinate change as an axis-aligned length depends on the orthogonal common-unit Cartesian metric convention.
Perpendicularity of the coordinate directions is the defining reason the auxiliary configuration is right-angled.

The coordinate configuration is what makes the general Pythagorean relation applicable to segment PQ; the theorem application itself is stated for any right triangle and is not blocked by the coordinate representation.
Correctly pairing x-coordinates with x-coordinates and y-coordinates with y-coordinates is definitionally required before corresponding coordinate separations can be expressed.
The auxiliary coordinate-aligned segments must preserve which ordered-pair components locate each endpoint.
Completing the route requires converting the squared-distance relation into the nonnegative distance formula by principal-root selection.
This is one complete standard way to demonstrate the strategy-neutral target, but ev001 does not establish the Pythagorean route as the only admissible derivation, so it is not a hard prerequisite.
The conventional result denotes a nonnegative distance as a principal square root, so isolating the nonnegative root is reliably blocking for the formula's final form.
Any coordinate-based derivation must preserve the defining horizontal and vertical roles of the ordered-pair components.

The distance formula is specifically the Euclidean metric relation of orthogonal, common-unit Cartesian coordinates, so that structure is definitional to the derived result rather than a curricular preference.

Producing a rule in the radical family presupposes the structural criterion for that family, so the target uses this concept; it is recorded as uses_concept rather than a hard prerequisite because classifying a separately supplied candidate rule is not a reliably blocking performance once the task establishes that the relationship is radical.

Each coefficient product must be returned to the power-of-ten scale of the place from which its coefficient came.

Reordering invariance is what licenses pairing terms in a more convenient order, though a particular execution may not reorder any terms.

Regrouping invariance is what licenses changing which partial sums are formed first, though not every execution regroups explicitly.
Determining the unnormalised same-unit counts is a reusable component of the specified place-value route.

Tens-and-ones decomposition supplies convenient additive parts for many mental restructurings, but other equivalent decompositions or plain reorderings may be used instead.
Property-based restructuring into convenient partial sums is a second complete admissible route to the same bounded target total.
Successive within-20 sums are one common route to a like-place count, but the count may also be shown concretely or reached by other accurate means, and counts through 39 exceed this atom's bound.
Interpreting each addend's components is the usual way the like-place counts become available, but a task may supply already grouped or componentwise quantities.
Coordinating and normalising like-place components is one complete admissible route to the target sum, explicitly authorised by the source but not mandated.
Small known sums are frequently used to form convenient partial sums, but partial sums in this target often exceed 20 and may be reached by other accurate means.
The place-value route coordinates each addend's tens and ones components, while the interpretation remains independently observable and reusable.
The tens-position count normally supplies the quantity to be normalised, although the composition can also be demonstrated on a supplied tens count.

Access to each addend's tens and ones underpins every place-value-based route, but the target admits mental methods that never expose the components explicitly, so this is not a blocking dependency.

Discriminating whether the presented number is positive or negative from its notation is the usual input-side step of the contextual mapping, but it is held as strong support rather than a hard gate because the polarity may be supplied verbally or by a label, in which case no separate notation-level classification performance is exercised.

The target's mathematical content is that a sign distinguishes two opposed contextual senses, so the oppositional structure of the situation is the concept the interpretation operates on; it is recorded as a concept-use relation rather than a gate because a task may present the opposed pair explicitly.

The target applies the situation's positive-versus-negative assignment to one particular number, so identifying that assignment is the strongest local support; it is not asserted as a hard prerequisite because the assignment may be displayed inside the target representation itself and need not be separately reported.

Identifying which of two opposed senses is positive and which is negative is definitionally about a pair of opposed senses: if the learner does not treat the two contextual senses as opposed, there is no binary correspondence to assign, so this dependency is definitional rather than merely instructional.

Contextual opposition is customarily introduced alongside or before sign notation, but the two are independent capabilities: notation-level polarity classification can be established without any situation, so only a weak ordering claim is made.
Recovering a parameter uses the established meanings of the base, equal-interval exponent, reference value, and baseline within the authorized exponential form.
Translating contextual facts into constraints supports context-based function writing but is not exercised when the relationship and its conditions are supplied symbolically or tabularly.
Single-parameter determination supplies a needed value when it is not directly given, but tasks may supply all parameters, so it is route-conditional support rather than a hard prerequisite.

The fixed multiplicative-factor structure is definitional of the object the learner must write; without it a produced rule cannot be reliably distinguished from an additive or otherwise nonexponential rule, so the dependency is definitional rather than merely instructional.

Interpreting a stated allowed-value restriction supports applying the domain clause of the satisfaction-set definition, but no separate restriction need be interpreted when the domain is already familiar and established.

Precedence and grouping judgments support instances presented as multi-operation expressions, but many problems state their relations sequentially or otherwise establish the calculation structure, so this is not a blocking dependency.

Addition of rational numbers is part of the operation coverage the target must support and is carried out inside the solution whenever the problem requires it; it is not asserted as a hard prerequisite because the target requires only whichever operations the particular problem needs.
Knowing the opposed contextual meanings of the two signs supports assigning correct signs when building a contextual arithmetic expression, but the convention may be stated directly by the task.
Multiplication of rational numbers is part of the target's operation coverage and is exercised inside the solution when the problem requires it, but no single operation is required in every instance.

Interpreting individual parts contextually prepares interpretation of a larger grouped entity, and the sources sequence the two, but a grouped portion can sometimes be contextualized holistically without separately interpreting every constituent.
